subject: computer-organization-and-architecture
subtopics: the instruction format: opcode and operand fields, fixed against variable length, byte alignment
the bit budget of a format: ceil(log2) for opcode, register and mode fields, and the remainder for the immediate
what an instruction set is: architecture against organisation, the four instruction families, RISC against CISC mode richness
zero-, one-, two- and three-address formats and the instruction count each costs
immediate addressing: the value in the instruction, no memory reference, source only
direct (absolute) addressing: the address in the instruction, one memory reference, field-width address space
indirect addressing: an address pointing at an address, two memory references, word-width reach, pointers
register and register-indirect addressing: no memory reference against one, and the pointer in a register
displacement addressing: indexed, base-register and base-with-index, EA = A + [R], records against arrays
PC-relative addressing and the branch offset arithmetic measured from the next instruction
autoincrement, autodecrement and stack addressing, with the increment equal to the item size
effective address and the memory-cycle count per mode, with fetch excluded from the execution cycle
program relocation and position-independent code: which modes survive a move and what has to be reloaded

chosen.title: Lecture 12 - Addressing Modes
chosen.channel: NPTEL, Computer Organization and Architecture - A Pedagogical Aspect (Prof. Jatindra Kr. Deka, Dr. Santosh Biswas, Dr. Arnab Sarkar, IIT Guwahati)
covers: the framing that an instruction needs an opcode and operands, and that the addressing mode is the rule for how the operands are present
the reason a high-precision operand is moved out of the instruction into memory: an immediate would lengthen the instruction
the immediate, direct, indirect, register and register-indirect ladder, with the size-and-speed trade-off of each rung
the statement that register addressing needs fewer bits and is faster but is limited by how few registers exist
displacement addressing as a two-part address, one part fixed in the instruction and one part in a register that can change
chosen.why: The only source read this run whose whole subject is this topic, and the only one that walks the modes as a ladder with the trade-off stated at each rung. It carries the definitions behind five cards: immediate, direct, indirect, register/register-indirect and the displacement framing. Read in part: the served extract runs from the opening through the first description of displacement addressing, so nothing is attributed to its indexed, relative, autoincrement or stack material.

chosen.title: Lecture 07 - Instruction Format and Addressing Modes
chosen.channel: NPTEL, Computer Organization and Architecture (Prof. Kamalika Datta, NIT Meghalaya)
covers: the opcode and operand parts of an instruction, worked on ADD R1, R2 and MOVE
the rule that a destination operand must be a register or a memory location while an immediate can only be a source
the zero- to three-address formats, with the note that the number of operands varies from instruction to instruction
the 32-bit field example in which 32 registers cost 5 bits each, and the enumeration of the mode list
the statement that load-store architectures support very few addressing modes, and that not every architecture has every mode
chosen.why: The only source read this run that states the destination-against-immediate rule and works a bit-budget example, which is what the format and bit-budget cards rest on. It is also the source that connects mode richness to load-store design. Read in part: the served extract runs from the opening through the list of mode names and the first sentences of the mode-by-mode teaching; nothing is attributed to the mode-by-mode section itself.

chosen.title: Lecture 3 - Instruction Set Architecture - 1
chosen.channel: NPTEL, Computer Architecture (Prof. Anshul Kumar, IIT Delhi)
covers: instructions as the interface between hardware and software, and as the primitive operations computation is described in
the design goals of an instruction set: express computation efficiently, maximise performance, minimise hardware cost and design time
the move from a toy machine to MIPS as a real and simple RISC architecture
the convention that the first listed register is the destination, which is a convention of the format rather than of the semantics
chosen.why: The only source read this run that frames the instruction set as a contract with stated design goals, which is what the ISA card needs and what neither of the two Guwahati lectures supplies in the readable part. Read in part: the served extract runs from the opening through the beginning of the arithmetic-instruction discussion.

chosen.title: Lecture 18 - Handling Different Addressing Modes
chosen.channel: NPTEL, Computer Organization and Architecture - A Pedagogical Aspect (IIT Guwahati)
covers: the three fetch micro-operations that are identical for every instruction, with the ALU incrementing the program counter during the fetch
the statement that from the fourth step onwards the control sequence depends on the addressing mode
the direct-mode sequence as IR -> MAR, memory read, MDR -> operand, which is one operand memory reference
the closing summary that a given instruction and mode determine a definite micro-operation sequence, and that different modes take different numbers of steps
chosen.why: The only source read this run that says why one mode costs more memory cycles than another - the control sequence itself changes - and it is the source behind the memory-cycle card's method of counting operations rather than recalling a table. Read in part: the opening, the direct-mode sequence and the closing summary were readable; the middle of the lecture, including the indirect and register-indirect sequences, was not, so nothing is attributed to it.

chosen.title: What is addressing modes in Hindi (addressing modes in hindi)
chosen.channel: computernetworksite.in - a Hindi article following the Stallings treatment of addressing modes
covers: the seven-mode taxonomy: immediate, direct, indirect, register, register indirect, displacement (relative, base register, indexing) and stack
the memory-reference cost of each mode, including that indirect needs three or more references for the whole instruction while direct needs one
the address-space reach of each mode, including that indirect reaches 2^N addresses for an N-bit word and register indirect is bounded by the register width
the advantage and disadvantage stated for every mode, which is the form a GATE matching question takes
displacement addressing split into relative, base register and indexing, with base holding a memory address and index holding a positive displacement
chosen.why: The only non-English source readable this run, and the only source that gives all seven modes with the memory-reference count and the address-space reach side by side - which is precisely the comparison GATE's matching and cycle-counting questions ask for. Read in part and translated into English here; every claim it contributes is recomputed in scripts/validate.py, because a translation sits between the source and the reader. Its instruction examples are 8085-specific and are not used. Two of its phrasings are loose against the standard treatment - it calls stack addressing 'implicit addressing' throughout, and its indirect count of 'three or more references' includes the instruction fetch - so the cards state the operand count (two) and say where the third reference comes from.

chosen.title: Computer Organization and Architecture web course, Module 4 - machine instructions, instruction format and addressing modes
chosen.channel: NPTEL web course by Prof. J. K. Deka, IIT Guwahati (read through a published mirror of the course pages)
covers: the architecture-against-organisation distinction, with the instruction set, data formats, I/O mechanisms and techniques for addressing memory listed as architectural attributes
the statement that Module 4 covers the architectural issues of addressing modes, machine instruction and instruction format in general rather than for one machine
the evolution-of-instruction-sets paragraph naming load/store designs and RISC as the simple-addressing machines and CISC as the complex ones
the course outline placing this material before the control-unit module, which is the order this topic's cards follow
chosen.why: The only source read this run that names the attributes an instruction set architecture consists of, which is what the ISA card is built on and what a definition question such as GATE CSE 2025 Set 2 Q.18 tests. Read in part: the outline and introduction chapters were readable through the mirror; the Module 4 chapter pages themselves were not in the returned extract, so no mode definition is attributed to this source.

standard_refs: Carl Hamacher, Zvonko Vranesic and Safwat Zaky, Computer Organization, chapter 2 - the addressing-mode list, the effective-address formulas and the memory-reference counts this topic is built on
David A. Patterson and John L. Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design, chapter 2 - instruction formats, the RISC mode set and the PC-relative branch offset measured from the next instruction
William Stallings, Computer Organization and Architecture, the addressing-modes chapter - the seven-mode taxonomy and the advantage and disadvantage of each, which the Hindi article follows
M. Morris Mano, Computer System Architecture - base-register addressing and program relocation, quoted on the GATE Overflow page for GATE CSE 1998 Q.1.19
GATE 2027 CS syllabus, Computer Organization and Architecture line 'Instruction set and addressing modes'
Official GATE CSE papers and answer keys for the fourteen recorded questions - not fetched this run, which is why every PYQ here is SOURCED rather than key-verified
notes: The syllabus names this topic in five words, 'Instruction set and addressing modes', so the thirteen subtopics above are this run's enumeration from the standard treatment (Hamacher's chapter 2, Stallings' mode chapter, the IIT Guwahati module 4 outline) and from the GATE question record - not a quotation from the syllabus. Every one of the thirteen has a card, which is why the status is not lower than partial; the gaps below are what keep it from being covered.

Fourteen GATE CSE previous-year questions were verified, from 1998 to 2026, and every one is SOURCED against an accepted answer rather than key-verified against an official key, so no marks field comes from an official key. Where a secondary site cites the official key (GATE 2024 CS2 Q.57 = 32, GATE 2025 CS1 Q.37 = 20) that is recorded in the answer_evidence and not upgraded to OFFICIAL_KEY, because the key document itself was not opened.

No video transcript was readable this run: two YouTube watch pages were fetched and carried no caption track, and the timedtext endpoint returned an empty body. So videoRefs is empty on all thirteen cards and no card quotes or timestamps a lecture. The six chosen sources are lecture transcripts, a web-course chapter and one article, all read as text.

One non-English source was readable, a Hindi article on the seven addressing modes, and it is marked translated on every card it feeds. It supplies the memory-reference counts, the address-space reach and the displacement split; every number it touches is recomputed in scripts/validate.py.

Four cards carry no previous-year question: the instruction-format card, the ISA card, the immediate card and the register card. Each says why in its source line rather than borrowing a question that does not test it - the format card's arithmetic is tested by the three bit-budget questions on the next card, and the immediate card's definition is the wrong option in GATE CSE 2002 Q.1.24.

Two questions of this topic are ambiguous as printed and the records say so instead of picking silently: GATE CSE 1999 Q.2.23 prints four options without saying more than one may be chosen while the accepted answer is all four, and GATE CSE 1998 Q.1.19 has answers arguing for base register addressing against the accepted PC-relative answer.

The naming of the displacement form is genuinely unstable across papers: GATE CSE 2011 Q.21 accepts 'Base Indexed' for 20(R2), GATE CSE 2017 Set 1 Q.11 accepts 'Index addressing mode' for X(R1), and GATE CSE 2026 Set 1 Q.4 distinguishes base-with-index from base-with-displacement. The card teaches EA = A + [R] and then says which label each paper used, rather than pretending one naming is correct.

The visual lesson animates one operand reached five ways from the same address field, so the memory-cycle counts and the direct-against-indirect distinction are shown on one memory picture. Every address, register value and cycle count in it is recomputed in scripts/validate.py.
